extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history and philosophy of science; readers interested in Bacon, Newton, and the development of scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Close historical-philosophical analysis of how Francis Bacon influenced the development and practice of experimental philosophy, and how that influence relates to figures such as Newton. The page enumerates modes of influence, methodological rules, and the present (educational) value of Bacon's logical works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popularisation of the study of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: He called men 'to lay themselves alongside of nature, to study her ways, and imitate her processes.' In one word, he popularised the study of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon publicly summoned wide audiences (rang the bell which called the other wits together), making the study of nature accessible and attractive beyond the narrow learned circles where it had previously been confined. The explanatory note contrasts whispering/learned books with Bacon's exhortations from the 'house-tops.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of experiment and observation
rubrics_metrics.description: He insisted, both by example and precept, on the importance of experiment as well as observation: 'Nature, like a witness, when put to the torture, would reveal her secrets.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimentation was present before Bacon but associated with alchemy; Bacon extended its range and dignity, giving it popularity and helping to shape institutional practice (e.g., Royal Society) and later work (Boyle, Newton). The passage emphasizes experimentation as a method that elicits facts from nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive study beyond natural facts (mind, conduct, society)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon's teaching extended the inductive study from external nature to the facts of mind, conduct, and society; 'The inductive study of Mental, Moral, and Political Philosophy' followed from his example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The influence is not limited to natural philosophy; Bacon's encouragement of factual, inductive inquiry influenced English thought in mental, moral, and political philosophy from the late seventeenth century onward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliverance from subjection to authority
rubrics_metrics.description: He sought to deliver men from the pernicious subjection to authority which had long enslaved thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon's rhetoric and program urged intellectual independence (likened in effect to Luther's role in religion). This criterion values breaking deference to traditional authorities as a precondition for genuine investigation. The text notes that this liberation was essential to the ensuing intellectual revolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emancipation of reason from imagination; rejection of unchecked hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Hypotheses non fingo' was a maxim Baconian in spirit — emancipation of reason from the bewitching enchantments of imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon warned against wild fancies and extravagance of suppositions when authority was removed; instead he invoked the 'majesty of facts.' The passage recommends examining premises themselves rather than merely deducing consequences from accepted premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic of Induction — induction presented with demonstrative force
rubrics_metrics.description: The most distinctive feature in Bacon's conception was that induction admitted of being presented with the force of demonstration and could supply as firm a basis for premises as syllogism supplies for conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon conceived of an inductive logic that is systematic and capable of rigorous demonstration if founded on true facts. The text cites Latin passages (e.g., Novum Organum Bk. I Aph. 105) and notes that this conception made inductive logic a foundational creation comparable to Aristotle's deductive logic, though requiring much later elaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection (not mere accumulation) of instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances require to be selected and not merely accumulated; selection of instances is the gist of inductive logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon emphasized the need to choose relevant, decisive instances (e.g., 'glaring instance', 'crucial instance', 'clandestine instance') and to establish principles for selecting and judging sufficiency; the passage notes that successors (Hooke, Herschel, Mill) repeated and reformulated these rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination of scientific enquiry to practical aims
rubrics_metrics.description: He insisted on subordinating scientific enquiries to practical aims — the furtherance of man's estate and the increase of comforts and conveniences of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon promoted applying intellectual efforts to improve material conditions. The text acknowledges that his view could be exaggerated but regards the practical orientation as largely beneficial in redirecting frivolous scholarly disputes toward useful investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hopefulness/optimism as an influential element
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon's hopefulness — belief that the future could be better and that present labours would improve the condition of following generations — was a key element of his influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optimism made Bacon persuasive and inspiring; the text presents his rhetorical vision (e.g., the sixth part of the Great Instauration) as motivating others to undertake long-term scientific labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical power and memorable diction as influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The marvellous language in which Bacon clothes his thoughts — grandeur, solemnity, majesty of diction — renders his teaching memorable and hard to criticise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon's phrasing ('Idols', 'Instances', aphorisms) is credited with lasting educational and motivational value; his style helps lodge ideas in memory and stimulates readers (compared to Shakespeare).

rubrics_metrics.name: Newton's 4th Rule (Regula) on propositions from phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule (Latin): 'In Philosophia experimentali, Propositiones ex phaenomenis per inductionem collectae, non obstantibus contrariis hypothesibus, pro veris aut accurate, aut quam proxime, haberi debent, donee alia occurrerint Phaenomena...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This Baconian-formulated rule (quoted in the text) says that in experimental philosophy, propositions collected from phenomena by induction should be held as true (or nearly true) until other phenomena require their amendment; objections must come from experiments or certain truths. The author argues the rule is thoroughly Baconian in substance and expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis before synthesis; experiments and induction as the method
rubrics_metrics.description: From the Optics passage: analysis (making experiments and observations and drawing conclusions by induction) ought ever to precede synthesis; hypotheses are not to be regarded in experimental philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage asserts that induction by enumeration is the method of analysis; while induction isn't demonstration, it's the best way of arguing permitted by the nature of things. If no exception occurs from phenomena, conclusions may be pronounced generally, but exceptions later modify them. The text notes Newton denies induction's force as demonstration, and seems to recognize only 'per enumerationem simplicem.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanations for Newton's silence regarding Bacon
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible accounts: (1) Bacon's reputation and principles were already so well established that explicit reference was superfluous; (2) contemporaneous authors rarely cite peers; (3) Newton's tastes lay more in mathematical science while Bacon was weak in mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author treats Newton's silence not as contempt but as explicable by historical habits of citation, established status of Baconian principles, and disciplinary preferences. This is offered as a rubric for interpreting absence of explicit attribution in historical figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present educational value of the Novum Organum (general effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The intrinsic value to the student: (1) general effect in guarding, stimulating, and disciplining the intellect; (2) the amount of definite logical doctrine in it which retains permanent value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As to (1), the First Book is highly stimulating for young readers and fosters habits of cautious, independent investigation. It teaches: take nothing on trust you can verify; examine first principles; be on guard against delusions from human nature, interests, the force of words, and tradition; form conclusions slowly and constantly check them by facts; avoid frivolous disputes; confine enquiries to solvable questions; subordinate investigations to human welfare. As to (2), the text is more cautious: some individual precepts remain valuable but others are antiquated and require modification; Bacon left much for successors to add and remodel.
